headings.title: Introduction and Fertility Return After Abortion
headings.content: Ovulation can resume as early as two weeks following an abortion, often before the first menstrual period returns. A common misconception among patients is that they cannot get pregnant until they experience a normal menstrual cycle. Nurses must clarify this timeline immediately during post-procedure care. Providing contraception before discharge prevents rapid repeat unintended pregnancies, which carry higher health risks.

headings.title: Client-Centered Contraceptive Counseling
headings.content:
- **Active listening**: Nurses must explore the patient's reproductive life plan without imposing personal biases.
- **Medical eligibility**: Assess underlying health conditions using standardized criteria before recommending specific methods.
- **Preference alignment**: Match the patient's lifestyle, bleeding profile tolerance, and future pregnancy desires with the right method.

headings.title: Immediate Versus Interval Contraceptive Initiation
headings.content: Immediate post-abortion contraception involves starting a chosen method before leaving the clinic or hospital on the same day as the procedure. Interval contraception delays initiation until a follow-up visit weeks later. Immediate initiation consistently lowers rates of repeat unintended pregnancies because patients may not return for scheduled follow-up visits.

headings.title: Long-Acting Reversible Contraception Options
headings.content: Long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) includes intrauterine devices (copper and hormonal) and subdermal implants. Both options can be safely inserted immediately following first- and second-trimester abortions. They offer high continuation rates and do not rely on daily user compliance.

headings.title: Hormonal and Barrier Contraceptive Methods
headings.content: Hormonal methods like injectables (Depo-Provera), combined oral contraceptive pills, and progestin-only pills offer reliable protection when used correctly. Barrier methods, including male and female condoms, protect against sexually transmitted infections alongside preventing pregnancy but have higher typical-use failure rates.

headings.title: Overcoming Barriers and Misconceptions
headings.content: Patients often harbor fears that modern contraceptives cause permanent infertility or severe weight gain. Nurses must debunk these myths using clear, empathetic education. Cultural stigma and partner disapproval also hinder uptake, requiring tailored counseling sessions that involve supportive partners when appropriate.

headings.title: Documentation and Follow-Up Care
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing documentation must record the chosen contraceptive method, patient understanding, and any side effect warnings provided. Follow-up appointments should be scheduled to assess satisfaction, check device placement if applicable, and manage any unexpected bleeding irregularities.
